 Indonesia's experts warn of powerful whirlwinds as rainy season begins
 November 16, 2026 11:56 GMT+700 
 Illustration – A total of 25 buildings and shops in Cibeureum Market, Ciwidey Subdistrict, Bandung District, West Java Province, were damaged by a whirlwind on Saturday (Nov. 14), according to the local disaster agency. 
 Jakarta (ANTARA) - The Indonesian Association of Disaster Experts (IABI) urged residents on Monday to prepare for whirlwinds as the rainy season begins, warning that wind speeds typically reach 60-120 km/h.
Daryono, head of IABI's communications, education and literacy division, said whirlwinds that struck West Lampung and other parts of Indonesia on Sunday underscored the need for extreme-weather preparedness.
A whirlwind is a compact, intense air vortex that typically lasts only briefly. Winds generally reach 60-120 km/h but can exceed 150 km/h in severe events, he said.
Strong surface heating, high humidity and atmospheric instability during seasonal transitions and early rainy-season conditions can fuel towering cumulonimbus (Cb) clouds, he said.
Not every Cb cloud produces a whirlwind. Formation requires specific conditions, including converging air masses, strong updrafts and rotation caused by winds blowing at different speeds and directions around the cloud.
Pressure and aerodynamic forces generated by the vortex can cause severe damage, lifting roofs, toppling trees and destroying poorly built structures, Daryono said.
Downbursts from Cb clouds can cause similar damage, he said, so field evidence is needed to distinguish the phenomena.
To reduce fatalities, residents should watch for warning signs such as towering dark clouds, sudden changes in wind direction or strength, and unusual rumbling sounds, he said.
"When winds intensify, shelter in a sturdy, permanent building's lowest-floor interior room, away from windows and lightweight roofs. Avoid trees, billboards, power poles and semi-permanent structures," Daryono said.
IABI said whirlwind preparedness must go beyond weather forecasts. Residents should reinforce roof connections, trim vulnerable tree branches and secure outdoor items that strong winds could carry away.
Local governments should strengthen radar-based early-warning systems in coordination with Indonesia's Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysics Agency (BMKG), speed up alerts and expand safety education because whirlwinds develop rapidly and locally.
"We cannot stop whirlwinds, but we can prevent them from becoming tragedies. Safety depends on sturdy buildings, recognizing threats and acting quickly to protect ourselves," Daryono said.
